stories.headline: Basildon Hospital gas and air halt 'completely unacceptable', says midwife union
stories.summary: The RCM says Basildon Hospital has had years to make gas and air safe for staff. Women in labour are offered alternative pain relief.
body: The Royal College of Midwives (RCM) says Basildon Hospital's managers have had years to make the maternity unit safe, and have not done it. The union says recent tests show nitrous oxide levels on the unit remain unsafe. It comes six weeks after the trust paid out to 121 staff who had been exposed to the gas.

Robbie Turner, the RCM's chief membership officer and deputy general secretary, said the safety problems with Entonox had left staff at risk. Now, he said, they were leaving women without safe and effective pain relief once more. "This is completely unacceptable," he said.

He said the union's health and safety reps at the hospital had been raising staff concerns about poor ventilation and leaking equipment. The RCM says it is disappointed that, rather than investing in better facilities and working with staff, the trust's decision simply reduces choice and the level of service for women.
## What the union wants
The RCM is urging the trust to find a long-term fix and to build it with staff and union reps. It says investment is needed urgently so the gas stays at safe levels across the whole maternity unit.
## What the trust says

In a letter to staff seen by the Daily Gazette, Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust said the unit will stop using gas and air from Thursday 26 November. It called it a "difficult decision". The trust says it has brought in specialist equipment and followed advice, but air-quality tests still sometimes show higher levels than it would like. Gas and air will not come back until there is a permanent solution, and the trust warned that could need a significant programme of building works.
## How we got here

The BBC reported on Monday that the decision came shortly after the trust's own specialist said a permanent fix to the unit's ventilation was a high priority. No date has been given for gas and air to return.

Figures released to the BBC under the Freedom of Information Act show the problem carried on into 2026. The legal workplace exposure limit was broken twice between January and July. Five people had raised readings in October, although the trust said none of those was over the limit. The trust says the unit is safe for families, and that the health risk is to staff who breathe the gas over long periods.

Concerns about gas levels on the unit were first raised in July 2021. An independent review by the Good Governance Institute found the trust should have treated them as a serious health risk from then, but did not do so until October 2022. The trust said in February 2024 that the review blamed weak governance, poor management of medical gases and unstable leadership. Its chief executive, Matthew Hopkins, apologised to staff and said it was "simply not acceptable that we took so long to act".

An internal hospital report found some staff breathed in up to 30 times the legal limit between 2021 and 2023. The BBC found staff were not told about test results showing the breaches for 16 months. In October, the trust settled claims from 121 staff, 85 of them midwives, for a total of £735,000, and apologised. It says some other claims are still outstanding.

The staff reported tiredness, anxiety, headaches and brain fog after long shifts on the unit. The Royal College of Midwives, which had more than 80 members among them, called it the largest group legal action ever brought by midwives in the UK. Daniel Poet of Thompsons Solicitors, who acted for most of the staff, told the BBC the trust knew about the danger in 2021 but did not tell staff for a year.

Entonox is a 50:50 mix of nitrous oxide and oxygen. The Health and Safety Executive sets a workplace limit for nitrous oxide of 100 parts per million, averaged over an eight-hour shift. It says high exposure can cause nerve problems and anaemia. It published new guidance on using the gas safely in maternity units in February 2025.

Basildon's maternity unit has stopped using the gas before. Basildon Nub News reported in December 2022 that Entonox was suspended there after a leak, while a new ventilation system was put in. The Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow also suspended gas and air in January 2023 after finding higher levels than usual, The Telegraph reported.

RCM reps raised concerns about ventilation and leaks
121 staff shared a £735,000 payout in October

stories.headline: Rochford Local Plan must go to inspector by 31 March, minister rules
stories.summary: Housing minister Matthew Pennycook wants Rochford's housing plan examined within months. He says the district has too little land set aside for homes.
body: Rochford District Council must send its Local Plan to a government inspector for examination by the end of March 2027, the BBC reported on Tuesday 24 November. In his letter to council leader Cllr Adi Malviya, housing minister Matthew Pennycook said he was "not convinced" by the council's reasons for removing six of its biggest housing sites. He also wants monthly progress reports until the plan is submitted.

The BBC's account of the letter sets out why the minister acted. Rochford has built 11% more homes than its targets required. But it has found less than two years' supply of land for new homes, when national rules expect five. Average house prices in the district are more than 11 times local earnings, against 7.6 times across England. Mr Pennycook said the policies in the district's last plan, adopted in December 2011, were likely to be significantly out of date.
## How we got here

The government has stepped in to make Rochford District Council push ahead with its plan for where new homes should go, after councillors cut out the largest housing sites. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook has ordered the council to put the plan out for public comment, in the version that still includes those sites.
## What is a Local Plan?

Every council is expected to have one. It is the rulebook for an area: it says where new homes, shops, jobs and roads can go, and council planners use it to decide planning applications. Rochford's covers the whole district, including Rayleigh, Rochford, Hockley, Hawkwell, Hullbridge, Ashingdon, Canewdon and Great Wakering, and runs up to 2043.

The district is still relying on old plans, from 2011 and 2014, which the council itself says are out of date. Until a new one is adopted, planning applications are decided against those and national planning rules.
## Why the government stepped in

Why so many homes? Under the government's new housing targets, Rochford's requirement was raised to 689 new homes a year, more than double the old figure, the council said in December 2025. At the time it said it wanted a plan "shaped by local evidence, local needs and local voices, not by arbitrary targets".

The Local Democracy Reporting Service reported that the draft put to councillors in September made room for 11,783 homes between 2026 and 2043. That is slightly more than the 11,710 the council had been asked to find land for. Almost half, 5,886, were on six large sites.

On 23 September councillors approved the plan only after removing all six of those sites, along with other changes suggested by a group of councillors. The vote was 13 for, none against and 19 abstentions. The council is run by a Reform UK minority administration.

A week later Mr Pennycook froze the plan with a "holding direction", an order stopping it going any further. According to Planning Geek's account of the letter, he said the changes left a significant shortfall against the district's identified housing need and risked a plan unlikely to pass examination. Council leader Cllr Adi Malviya asked for an urgent meeting and later urged ministers to lift the freeze, [as The Seax reported](/story/rochford-local-plan-holding-direction-christmas/), warning that a consultation could end up running over Christmas.
## What ministers have ordered now

Mr Pennycook wrote to Cllr Malviya on Monday 23 November. He told the council to start the consultation on 7 December, using the version of the plan put to councillors before they took the six sites out. The council may not withdraw the plan, must report to ministry officials every month and must see it through to the end. Small changes are allowed after the consultation, but any big change has to go to the Secretary of State.
## What it means for residents

The consultation is the public's chance to comment. At this late stage, comments have to be about whether the plan is legally compliant and sound, meaning workable and properly justified. Objections to particular sites can still be made on those grounds. After that, a planning inspector appointed by the government examines the plan before it can be adopted. The council has not said how long the consultation will run; in September it planned six weeks. Earlier this month it said the plan had to be submitted by 31 December, though Cllr Malviya said the government had indicated the deadline could move to March. The minister's letter has now fixed it at the end of March 2027.
"Many people in our district feel strongly about the Local Plan," Cllr Malviya said. The council says it is considering how to respond to the letter and will update residents in the coming days.
points: Plan makes room for about 11,800 homes across the district by 2043
Public consultation on the full plan starts on 7 December
Council cannot withdraw it and must report to ministry officials every month
Leader: 'Many people in our district feel strongly about the Local Plan'

stories.headline: Cold Norton: police find £300,000 cannabis farm in barn
stories.summary: Officers found more than 500 plants near Cold Norton after a tip-off. Police say grows like this can be linked to modern slavery.
body: Maldon's neighbourhood policing team uncovered the cannabis grow in a barn in the Cold Norton area on Sunday 22 November, Essex Police said. Officers went there after a tip from UK Power Networks, the company that runs the local electricity network. The force estimates the plants are worth £300,000 on the street.

Pictures released by the force show rows of tall plants under hanging lamps, with ducting and cables strung across the roof. A body-worn camera image shows a narrow corridor between growing areas lit in yellow. A forensic investigator in a white suit is pictured at the scene.
Police have not said whether anyone has been arrested.
Sergeant Dalby said his team would keep targeting cannabis farms across the Maldon district. He warned that large grows like this 'can be linked to organised crime, modern slavery and forced labour'.

Cold Norton is a small village on the Dengie peninsula, south of Maldon. In June, officers from the Maldon and Chelmsford teams seized 681 cannabis plants, valued by police at £500,000, from an industrial unit off Latchingdon Road in the village.
Anyone who sees something they think may be linked to growing, making or dealing drugs can report it to Essex Police on its website.
points: Barn searched on Sunday 22 November
Tip-off came from UK Power Networks
Report suspected drug activity at essex.police.uk

stories.headline: Colchester's ROL Cruise named UK's third best company to work for
stories.summary: A Colchester holiday firm has climbed into the UK's top three workplaces. The ranking is based on what its own staff say.
body: ROL Cruise, the independent cruise specialist based in Colchester, finished third in the 2026 Best Companies league table, the company said on Tuesday 24 November. It came fourth in 2025, its first year in the rankings.
The firm was also named the top employer in hospitality and leisure. Chief executive Rosie Cairns said the result "belongs to every member of the team".

Top employer in hospitality and leisure
Second best mid-sized company in the UK

stories.headline: Basildon business support scheme ranked in UK's top four for impact
stories.summary: A Basildon scheme for new and growing firms has won national recognition. It did so on a fraction of its rivals' budgets.
body: The Consortium (East) Ltd was placed among the top four in the Outstanding Impact category of the Institute of Economic Development's 2026 awards. It was shortlisted for Elevate Basildon Business, which Basildon Borough Council paid for in 2025/26 with UK Shared Prosperity Fund money.
The firm said the programme reached 342 people, helped start 55 businesses and supported 29 new jobs. Greater Manchester Growth Hub came first.

Funded by the UK Shared Prosperity Fund
Greater Manchester Growth Hub won the category

stories.headline: Hatfield Peverel man, 26, jailed for five years for sexual assaults
stories.summary: David Cooney is now on the sex offenders' register. The woman he assaulted says she finally has closure.
body: David Cooney, 26, of Church Road, Hatfield Peverel, was jailed for five years at Chelmsford Crown Court on Tuesday 17 November, Essex Police said. He was also placed on the sex offenders' register indefinitely.

The woman he assaulted says her 'world was destroyed' by what he did. In a statement released by the force, she said: 'He got what he deserved. I feel like he tried to ruin my life and my reputation.'
'I was very mentally unwell after what he did to me,' she said. 'It affected every area of my life. I lost my home and everything fell apart.'
## How the case unfolded

An investigation began in 2022, after the woman reported a sexual assault. Cooney was arrested on suspicion of rape, attempted rape and sexual assault. He denied the allegations when detectives interviewed him.
Detectives charged him with all three offences. At a trial in August 2025, a jury found him not guilty of rape and attempted rape. That jury was discharged on the other counts.
A retrial was held at Chelmsford Crown Court in October. This time the jury found him guilty of two counts of sexual assault by penetration.
## 'Consequences are very clear'

She found the court process hard, she said. But she praised the investigating officer, Detective Sergeant Jade Lawton, and her independent sexual violence advisers, Jemma and Claire. 'What an amazing job they did,' she said.
She also thanked her family for believing in her over four years, and herself 'for not giving up'.
'My attacker thought he could just sexually assault me, take what he wanted without consequences,' she said. 'Well this week the consequences of those actions are very clear.'
## 'True strength'

Det Sgt Lawton said the woman had shown 'true strength' through a long investigation. She had no faith in the police before the assault, the officer said, so reporting it and staying with the case 'was no mean feat'.

'She stood up to the perpetrator by coming to the police and has prevented him from hurting anyone else,' Det Sgt Lawton said. She urged anyone struggling with something similar to reach out to support services.
## Where to get help

Synergy Essex offers free, confidential support to anyone affected by rape, sexual abuse or sexual violence, whether it happened recently or long ago. You do not need to report it to the police first.

Its services include counselling in person, online or by phone, practical and emotional help, and independent sexual violence advisers. Its First Contact Navigator team can help with next steps on 0300 003 7777.
By law, the woman has lifelong anonymity.
points: Sentenced on Tuesday 17 November
Cleared of rape and attempted rape at a 2025 trial
Free support: Synergy Essex, 0300 003 7777

stories.headline: Epping Forest council crushes fly-tipping truck in a first for the district
stories.summary: A truck linked to a large fly-tip on Epping Forest heathland has been crushed. It is the council's first use of the power.
body: Epping Forest District Council crushed the Ford Transit truck on 11 November and announced it on Tuesday 24 November. It is the first vehicle the council has seized and destroyed over fly-tipping and illegal waste offences in the district.

According to the council, the truck was involved in a fly-tip in January, when more than a tonne of construction and demolition waste was dumped on heathland in the forest. It was seized in August after its driver was arrested on a separate matter.

The City of London Corporation, which owns and manages Epping Forest, spotted the truck's link to the January dump and contacted the district council. The council holds the legal power to seize and keep vehicles, and Essex Police helped with the operation.
## A tougher line on dumping

Councillor Darshan Sunger, the council's portfolio holder for public protection and environment, said crushing the truck sent a clear message. "We will not hesitate to do it again," he said. He added that the council would use CCTV, fines and vehicle seizures against offenders, and would prosecute where it had evidence.

Councils have been given renewed government guidance urging them to destroy vehicles used for illegal dumping, the council said. It warned that fly-tippers risk fines of up to £5,000 as well as losing their vehicles. Earlier in November, a motion to full council asked for the district's top fixed penalty to rise from £1,000, [as The Seax reported](/story/cw-epping-fly-tipping-fine-5000-motion/).
## How to report it

Anyone who sees fly-tipping should not confront the people involved or touch the waste, which can hide broken glass, needles or asbestos. A crime happening now should be reported on 999. Dumped waste can be reported to the council online at any time, or on 01992 564000 during office hours.
points: Truck seized in August, months after the January dump
City of London Corporation and Essex Police helped
Report fly-tipping on 01992 564000

stories.headline: Chelmsford bus C3 to reach Boreham and Beaulieu Park station in January
stories.summary: Chelmsford's C3 bus will link Boreham with the new Beaulieu Park station. A Sunday route and an extra hospital shift trip are also coming.
body: First Bus will change its Essex network on Sunday 3 January 2027, with most of the changes in and around Chelmsford. Its C3 service is being extended to Boreham. That gives the village a bus to Beaulieu Park station in the morning and evening peaks from Monday to Saturday, and all day on Sundays.
Beaulieu Park is Chelmsford's new station on the Great Eastern main line. First Bus says the longer route will make it easier for commuters to catch trains towards Chelmsford, Colchester and London.
## Sunday service and hospital shifts

A new Sunday route, the C3A, will also start. It will run from Beeleigh Link, in the Chelmer Village development east of Chelmsford, through Boreham and the city centre to North Melbourne in the west.
On Saturdays the C2 gets one extra journey. It is timed to fit shift changeovers at Broomfield Hospital, so more staff can get to and from work by bus.
In Colchester, route 520 will be renumbered 320. First Bus says the new number is meant to make travel simpler for passengers.

Julian Elliott, head of network for First Bus in the East and Midlands, said the company had listened to customer feedback before planning the changes. He said they should help people "travel to work more easily around Chelmsford and Colchester".
## What happens next
Full timetables for each route are on the First Bus Essex website. Passengers who use the C2, C3 or 520 can check their times there before the changes start.
points: New C3A runs on Sundays from Beeleigh Link to North Melbourne
One extra Saturday C2 trip for Broomfield Hospital shifts
Colchester's 520 becomes the 320

stories.headline: Epping nurse Tracy Reed honoured for 27 years in community care
stories.summary: A west Essex nurse has won a national long service award. She joined the NHS as a clerk at 17.
body: Tracy Reed is clinical lead for end-of-life care at Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust (EPUT). She has received the Long Service Award from the Queen's Institute of Community Nursing, a charity that works to improve nursing care for people at home. EPUT announced the award on Tuesday 24 November. She has spent more than 27 years in community nursing and 45 years in the NHS.

Her career began at Warley Hospital, where she worked as an administrative clerk. Her mum and sister were both nurses, but she had not thought of joining them. That changed after a first aid course, when she found herself helping a person who was having a heart attack.
## A career across west Essex

She went on to train as a nurse and worked in general medicine, coronary care, community nursing and care of older people. For the last 15 years she has specialised in end-of-life care. Much of her career was spent in west Essex, at St Margaret's Hospital in Epping, the Herts and Essex Hospital and Princess Alexandra Hospital in Harlow, and in the Epping, Loughton and Stansted communities. For the past 12 years she has worked across the county.

Ms Reed has been a Queen's Nurse since 2012, a title the institute gives to nurses who show a high level of commitment to patient care. She volunteered twice in Nepal after its devastating earthquake and has kept supporting health projects there. She is also an independent adviser on end-of-life care for the Motor Neurone Disease Association and a Macmillan Professional with Macmillan Cancer Support.
"I realised a long time ago being a nurse is not what I do but who I am," she said. She added that she felt lucky to have cared for and worked with so many people.
points: Queen's Nurse since 2012
Specialised in end-of-life care for 15 years
Volunteered in Nepal after the 2015 earthquake
stories.source: Essex Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust

stories.headline: Harlow family centre Savannah Lodge gets new Ofsted notice after visit
stories.summary: Savannah Lodge in Harlow has improved since Ofsted rated it inadequate in July. One safeguarding notice is still not met.
body: Ofsted inspectors made a follow-up visit to the residential family assessment centre in Fir Park, Harlow, after a full inspection on 22 July 2026 rated it inadequate. That inspection raised serious concerns about safeguarding and leadership. It led to two compliance notices and a limit on how many families the centre could take, Your Harlow reported on Tuesday 24 November.

One notice has now been met. A fresh notice was issued on the other, and Ofsted will visit again. Inspectors found refurbished bedrooms and better records of incidents, but said a new safeguarding policy was unclear.
points: Bedrooms now have new furniture, cots and mattresses
No internal audits by the responsible individual yet
Families said they would feel able to complain

stories.headline: Grays' Essex Fire Museum wins Best Museum at Essex Mums Awards
stories.summary: The free museum at a working Grays fire station beat strong competition, including Essex Police's museum in Chelmsford.
body: Essex Fire Museum was named Best Museum for 2026 at the Essex Mums Awards, Your Harlow reported on Tuesday 24 November. It shows vintage fire engines, uniforms and equipment from three centuries, and volunteers use a mock house to point out fire risks.

Dan Bailey, heritage and volunteering lead at Essex County Fire and Rescue Service, thanked the volunteers who host school, scout and family visits. Entry is free, but visits must be booked by email because the museum sits on an operational fire station.

Christmas open day on Sunday 13 December

stories.headline: Elsenham airport car park told to close by February after appeal fails
stories.summary: The unauthorised Stansted parking site at New Farm has lost its fight with the council. The land must now be cleared.
body: A planning inspector has dismissed most of an appeal against Uttlesford District Council's order to close the car park at New Farm, off Stansted Road in Elsenham. The ruling, published on Monday 23 November, gives the operator until 23 February 2027 to stop parking and storing vehicles on the land. The cars, shipping containers and hard standing must go, and the land must be put back as it was.

BBC News reported that the inspector, Graeme Robbie, upheld the enforcement notice but turned down a request for six months to wind the business down. He extended the time allowed to comply from two months to three. The appeal said the business had future bookings to honour, and that cancelling them would hurt the company and its customers.
## How we got here

The site, on former farmland beside the M11, began offering cheaper parking for Stansted passengers in early 2025. The council served its enforcement notice on 14 August 2025, after talks failed to persuade the operator to stop voluntarily. SC Parking Ltd appealed on 1 September 2025, the Bishop's Stortford Independent reported, and the notice was suspended while the Planning Inspectorate considered the case.

The car park kept growing in the meantime. A BBC investigation, reported in July, found it had expanded by almost two-thirds since the summer of 2025, with room for about 1,000 vehicles. Residents complained of diggers excavating more land. Customers reported long waits, crowded shuttle vans and cars returned dirty or damaged.
## What happens next

Uttlesford District Council said it would keep monitoring the site and work to make sure the operator complies within the inspector's timescale. In September the Bishop's Stortford Independent reported that if the notice was upheld and then ignored, the council could consider further enforcement, including prosecution. Stansted Airport has advised passengers to check that a parking firm is reputable before they book. The operators did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
points: Inspector refused a six-month wind-down
Enforcement notice first served in August 2025
Site can hold about 1,000 vehicles, the BBC estimated

stories.headline: Stansted Airport rehearses plane crash response with 400 people
stories.summary: The blue lights around the airport on Tuesday 24 November were only a drill. Flights were planned to run as normal.
body: Anyone near London Stansted on Tuesday 24 November may have seen a large number of emergency vehicles. The airport was running a full-scale training exercise that simulated a major aircraft accident, to check how its teams and the emergency services would cope with the real thing.

The drill took place at Compass Base, a remote aircraft parking stand away from the terminal, using a decommissioned aircraft. The airport said it had been planned so there is no impact on flights or passengers. Civil Aviation Authority rules require every UK certificated aerodrome to stage an exercise like this at least once every four years.

About 400 people took part. Airport teams worked alongside Essex Police, Essex County Fire and Rescue Service, the East of England Ambulance Service and Essex & Herts Air Ambulance. The British Red Cross, Uttlesford District Council and Essex County Council also supported it. So did the Rapid Relief Team, the Air Accidents Investigation Branch and the housing ministry, along with Ryanair, Border Force and National Express.

The scenario called for a long and complicated response involving many organisations. It was designed to test life-saving procedures, who takes command and how, communications, and the support offered to passengers, their families and others caught up in it.

Nick Millar, operations director at London Stansted, said an aircraft accident was "an extremely unlikely event". He added that it "remains the most significant emergency scenario we could face", so the plans must be tested regularly. He said the exercise would let the airport rehearse how it works with partners in a highly challenging situation and find ways to strengthen its response.

Chief Inspector Julia Finch, Essex Police's Stansted Airport commander, said: "We regularly test our plans and capabilities, and this is no exception." She said exercises like this make sure the force is ready for any eventuality, however unlikely, and that it has a really positive working relationship with the airport.
points: A decommissioned aircraft was used on a remote stand
The Civil Aviation Authority requires a full-scale drill every four years
Ryanair, Border Force and the British Red Cross were among those helping
stories.newAngle: the exercise is taking place today, Tuesday 24 November

stories.headline: Tolleshunt D'Arcy village hall wins £70,000 for January refit
stories.summary: Tolleshunt D'Arcy's century-old village hall has secured grants for its long-awaited repairs, years after a bid to replace the building outright fell through.
body: Work on the floors, the stage and the storage areas of Tolleshunt D'Arcy Village Hall is due to begin in January, Essex County News reported on Tuesday 24 November. The grant money will pay for the next stage of a refurbishment that villagers have been planning for years.
## A long road

Tolleshunt D'Arcy Parish Council's project page tells the story. A parish survey by the Rural Community Council for Essex reported in 2018, and a charity trust with seven trustees took over running the hall in April 2019. Its first plan was a new building. The trustees bid for £870,000 from The National Lottery's Reaching Communities programme, but the bid failed.

Planning permission for a new hall was granted in August 2021. By October 2022 the estimated cost of a new build had risen to between £1.04m and £1.1m. The trustees then chose to refurbish the existing hall in stages instead.

Their plan has five phases, starting with the main hall, foyer and toilets. It includes insulating the floors and roofs, new windows and doors, and probable rewiring. Local help has played its part: D&D Engineering of Tollesbury refitted the kitchen free of charge, and volunteers from Ford UK painted the main hall and kitchen in 2022.
points: Lottery bid for £870,000 failed
A new build would have cost up to £1.1m
Hall run by a charity trust since April 2019

stories.headline: Southend Airport hunts first Chief Christmas Officer with Lapland prize
stories.summary: London Southend Airport is looking for its first Chief Christmas Officer, and the winner and a guest fly to Lapland for the day on 22 December.
body: There is no CV and no interview. To apply, people post a short video on Instagram or TikTok saying why they deserve the job, using the hashtag #LSAChiefChristmasOfficer. Breaking Travel News reported that entries opened on Friday 20 November.
London Southend Airport is running the competition with tour operator The Lapland Experience. The best videos will be shared on both firms' social media, and the winner will be named on 11 December.
## The prize

On the day, the winner and a guest fly from Southend to Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland and are home the same evening. Their day includes huskies, reindeer, a one-to-one meeting with Santa and a visit to Santa Claus Village. The flight takes about three hours, according to the airport's own page.
Nigel Mayes, the airport's business development director, said the idea was to capture the excitement of Christmas and show off its Lapland flights.
## Lapland from Southend
The Lapland Experience announced its Southend day trips in March. It said its earlier trips had flown from other airports.
points: Entries are videos on Instagram or TikTok
Winner named on Friday 11 December
Flight to Rovaniemi takes about three hours

stories.headline: Brentwood and Rochford invite businesses to become Safe Spaces for women
stories.summary: Both councils are holding drop-in events through the 16 Days of Activism against gender-based violence to recruit businesses and community groups to the Women's Safety Charter.
body: Businesses and community groups in Brentwood and Rochford district are being asked to become places where women and girls can go for help. Both councils launched drives on Monday 23 November to sign up more organisations to the Women's Safety Charter. Rochford District Council calls it a county-wide scheme.
## What a Safe Space is

Organisations that join can be accredited as Safe Spaces: visible places where a woman or girl who feels unsafe can ask for help. Their staff get guidance and training on how to respond, Brentwood Borough Council says. The charter also backs White Ribbon, the campaign that asks men and boys to challenge harmful attitudes.
## Drop-ins in Brentwood

The events run through the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, an international campaign that starts on Wednesday 25 November and ends on 10 December. Brentwood's first drop-in is at Unit 10 in the Baytree Centre that Wednesday, from 10am to noon. The second is outside Marks & Spencer on the High Street on 3 December, also in the morning. The last is back at the Baytree Centre on 10 December, from 2pm to 4pm.

Essex Police, Victim Support, Changing Pathways, Renew Counselling, Phoenix Futures, Active Essex and Essex County Fire and Rescue Service will be there, with the council's housing team. Councillor Dr Tim Barrett chairs the council's housing, health and community committee. He said the council was working with local organisations and businesses "to create safer spaces".
## Drop-ins in Rochford district

Rochford's events start at The Mill Arts and Events Centre in Rayleigh on 25 November, then move to Clements Hall Leisure Centre in Hawkwell on 3 December. Both run from 2pm to 4pm. The last is outside the Star Café pie and mash shop on Rayleigh High Street on 10 December, from 10am to noon.

Essex Police, Active Essex, Phoenix Futures, Bar 'n' Bus and Sanctuary Housing are joining the council's domestic abuse and community safety teams. Councillor Jo McPherson, who chairs Rochford's community and housing committee, urged residents to "come along to our events" and meet the organisations involved.
## How it started

Brentwood has been working on this for at least two years. In November 2024 it ran a survey with the charter asking women how safe they feel across the borough, with a focus on specific male behaviours. Tendring District Council unveiled its own Women's Safety Charter to businesses in February 2026, paid for by the Essex Police, Fire and Crime Commissioner's Safer Streets programme.
## How to join
Organisations can find out more at brentwood.gov.uk/womens-safety-charter and rochford.gov.uk/womens-safety-charter. Anyone in immediate danger should call 999.
points: Accredited Safe Spaces get staff training on how to help
Events at the Baytree Centre, Rayleigh and Hawkwell
Essex Police and Victim Support among those taking part

stories.headline: Chelmsford MP backs Paul's Law after Birch care home choking death
stories.summary: Marie Goldman wants every care worker trained to spot and manage swallowing problems, after a jury found failures in the care of Paul Spearing, who choked on unsuitable food at his care home near Colchester and died in November 2023.
body: Ms Goldman, the Liberal Democrat MP for Chelmsford, and Barking's Labour MP Nesil Caliskan wrote to Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper on Thursday 19 November. They want national training on dysphagia, cerebral ataxia and choking risks written into the government's coming Social Care Workforce Action Plan, and Care Quality Commission rules updated to match. The campaign, launched by Paul's family, is called Paul's Law.
## The law now

Care providers in England must already make sure their staff are properly trained. But there is no national training standard for care workers on dysphagia awareness or choking prevention, the MPs' letter says. Dysphagia is a condition that makes swallowing food and drink unsafe.
## What happened to Paul

Paul Spearing had cerebral palsy, a learning disability, autism, cerebral ataxia and dysphagia. He had lived for more than 20 years at a home run by Essex Care Consortium in Birch, needed one-to-one care day and night, and relied on staff for everything he ate and drank.

Speech and language therapists had advised in 2018 and 2019 that he must not have mixed-texture food or thin drinks such as milk. At breakfast on 12 November 2023 he was given a croissant softened in milk and choked. He died at Colchester General Hospital three days later, aged 41.
## What the jury found

An eight-day inquest at Essex Coroner's Court, before Senior Coroner Sonia Hayes, ended on Friday 11 September. The jury found the meal broke his speech and language guidance and caused his death. It said the home's mealtime guidance was inadequate and inconsistent, and staff did not know his needs well enough.

His assessment called dysphagia training essential, but not everyone caring for him had been given it. The jury heard the course cost £14 a person, while the home was paid £3,672 a week for his care, his family's barristers' chambers, 1 Crown Office Row, reported. The jury also found his room, in a separate pod, was not linked to the emergency buzzer system, which delayed first aid.

The coroner ruled that Article 2 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the right to life, applied. That means an inquest looks more widely at how a death happened. The MPs say this is unusual for a privately run care home, and they have asked the Department of Health and Social Care to consider what families lose when it is not applied.
## The petition

A petition on the UK Parliament website, started by Rachel Uddin, asks for compulsory dysphagia training for staff supporting people with learning disabilities and other vulnerable adults. It says the condition affects one in five older adults. It opened on Tuesday 17 November and had 425 signatures by the evening of 23 November. The government replies to petitions that reach 10,000 signatures, and Parliament considers a debate at 100,000.
Sharing the letter on Facebook, Ms Goldman said: "No family should have to endure what Paul's family has."
points: The petition runs until 17 May 2027
The letter asks for CQC regulation to change as well as training
The care home's procedure for sharing a buzzer delayed help, the jury found

stories.headline: QEII bridge reopens after police incident adds to a torrid day at Dartford
stories.summary: Everything was open again by 6.20pm, but drivers going both ways faced hours of queues, and more overnight closures follow this week.
body: It was a day of delays at the Dartford Crossing, the main road link between Essex and Kent, on Monday 23 November. First, an urgent repair kept the east tunnel, which carries traffic into Essex, shut for more than nine hours longer than planned. Then, in the evening rush hour, a police incident closed the Queen Elizabeth II Bridge, which carries traffic into Kent.
## How the crossing works

Traffic heading north into Essex uses two tunnels: the east tunnel and the smaller west tunnel, which has a 4.8m height limit. Traffic heading south into Kent goes over the bridge. When one of them shuts, everything has to squeeze through what is left.
## Morning: the tunnel repair

National Highways said damage to an expansion joint just in front of the east tunnel entrance was found during planned overnight work. The tunnel was due to reopen at 5am but stayed shut while specialist crews repaired the joint through the morning and into the afternoon. National Highways said in an update at about 2.40pm that traffic was flowing through both tunnels again.

While it was shut, every driver heading for Essex had to use the west tunnel. KentOnline reported morning queues back to junction 3 of the M25 at Swanley and along the London-bound A2 past Gravesend, and Ensignbus cancelled its 9.05am service from Lakeside and its 9.30am journey from Bluewater. Even after the reopening, National Highways warned of seven miles of queues on the anticlockwise M25, back from junction 4 for Orpington.
## Evening: the bridge closure

At around 5.30pm the bridge was closed southbound for a police-led incident, with Essex Police leading the response at the scene. By about 6.10pm National Highways was reporting delays of 60 minutes and about four miles of congestion on the approach. A National Highways traffic camera showed long tailbacks at 6.06pm.

Police released the traffic at about 6.20pm and all lanes reopened, National Highways said in its final update. It warned that leftover delays of more than 60 minutes would take time to ease. Neither National Highways nor police have said what the incident was.
## More closures this week

The west tunnel is booked to shut overnight, from 9pm to 5.30am, between Monday 23 and Thursday 26 November for maintenance, according to National Highways' Dartford Crossing works page. The west tunnel also shuts from 10pm to 5.30am on Saturday 28 November, and the east tunnel from 10.30pm to 5.30am on Sunday 29 November, the Evening Standard's live coverage reported.
points: East tunnel into Essex stayed shut until mid-afternoon for urgent repairs
Bridge into Kent closed for nearly an hour in the evening rush
West tunnel shuts overnight, 9pm to 5.30am, until Thursday

stories.headline: South Essex father jailed for abusing his two vulnerable children
stories.warning: this story contains details of child abuse that some readers may find distressing. Where to get help is listed at the end.
stories.summary: Detectives showed him video of what he had done, and a judge called it "gratuitous degradation". The children's mother, who delayed telling police, was given a community order.
body: A father from south Essex has been jailed for four years and nine months for abusing his two young children, who have additional and complex care needs. He admitted two counts of child cruelty and one of intentional suffocation and was sentenced at Basildon Crown Court on Monday 23 November. He will be on an extended licence of three years when he is released, Essex Police said.

Police said evidence showed he repeatedly physically abused the children in the family home, including an incident in which one child was suffocated. The force has chosen not to name either parent. It said this was not to protect them but to protect the children's anonymity and wellbeing.
## The mother

The children's mother admitted two counts of child neglect, which related to her delay in telling police what she knew was happening. Police said she was aware of abusive behaviour towards the children but failed to protect them before eventually contacting officers in December 2025. She was given a two-year community order with 150 hours of unpaid work.
## The investigation

Both parents were arrested and the case went to Essex Police's Child Abuse Investigation Team. In interview the father at first played down his behaviour and denied that it amounted to abuse, until detectives showed him video evidence recovered during the investigation. Detective Constable Scott Cameron told him the recording had "shocked me to my core", and that the only thing more shocking was his lack of reaction while watching it. Faced with the evidence, the father admitted the offences.

DC Courtney White, who led the investigation, said the children "should have been able to depend upon the adults around them to keep them safe". She said detectives examine distressing evidence in painstaking detail because abused children "may not always be able to tell somebody what is happening to them".
## The judge

Sentencing, His Honour Judge Collery KC told the father he appeared to be "seeking to torment the children" and described what happened as "gratuitous degradation, which could almost be said to be sadistic". He told him he was dangerous and presented a substantial risk of causing serious harm to children in the future.
## Where to get help

Anyone worried that a child is being abused can call Essex Police on 101, or 999 in an emergency, or the NSPCC helpline on 0808 800 5000. Children and young people can call Childline free, any time, on 0800 1111.

He faces an extended licence of three years on release
Police chose not to name the parents to protect the children
Both children now live in a safe and loving home, police say

stories.headline: Epping Forest district's 50 favourite trees go on show at museum
stories.summary: Residents' choice of the 50 best-loved trees in the Epping Forest district is now on display at Epping Forest District Museum, marking 40 years of the council's Countrycare team.
body: Nominations came in from across the district throughout 2026, and the exhibition opened on Saturday 21 November with photographs and personal stories behind each choice. It was created by the council's Countrycare service with the charity that runs the museum.

Councillor Darshan Sunger, the council's cabinet member for Countrycare, said people chose trees for family links, history, location and size as well as their value to wildlife. The display sits in the museum's central stairwell.

The exhibition runs until 14 April 2027. Countrycare was set up in 1986 to look after habitats, improve access to the countryside and give advice on nature conservation and wildlife law in the district.
points: Nominations ran through 2026
Countrycare marks its 40th anniversary
Free to see in the museum's central stairwell

stories.headline: Thaw Patrol and Snow Be Gone Kenobi join Essex gritting fleet
stories.summary: Essex's gritters are ready for winter. New lorries with playful names join the fleet that keeps main roads moving in ice and snow.
body: Essex Highways has 55 gritting lorries fitted with snow ploughs ready for the winter, plus two mini spreaders. Twenty-one of the lorries are new, the Bishop's Stortford Independent reported on Monday 23 November. Their names include The Snowy Way is Essex, Thaw Patrol and Snow Be Gone Kenobi.

Each gritting run covers more than 2,000 miles of road, about 40% of the county's network, across 51 routes. Main roads come first. So do bus routes with four or more buses a day each way, and the roads to hospitals and schools. Around 104 drivers share the work, and most of them normally work on road maintenance crews.
## How the decision to grit is made

Forecasters send Essex Highways a daily report with the lowest expected temperatures and any risk of frost, black ice or snow. Decision makers then choose whether and when to grit, usually at lunchtime, so roads are treated before frost forms. That decision is posted on X by @EssexHighways with the tag #EssexGritters.
Lorries usually go out between 2am and 5am, between 7pm and 10pm, or both. A priority route takes about three hours to finish. Last winter the fleet gritted more than 120,000 miles of road.

Councillor Mark Webster, Essex County Council's cabinet member for highways and infrastructure, said: "Our weather can change quickly." Drivers can see where the lorries are on the Track the gritters map on the Essex Highways website, which also lists every salting route.
points: 51 routes, with main roads, busy bus routes, hospitals and schools first
About 104 drivers, mostly from road maintenance crews
Runs usually 2am to 5am or 7pm to 10pm

stories.headline: Stansted Airport links 140+ local firms to its terminal expansion work
stories.summary: Local businesses met buyers at London Stansted's 25th Meet the Buyers event, as the airport looks for suppliers for its five-year terminal transformation.
body: The firms held 700 one-to-one meetings with 30 buyers and procurement specialists at the Radisson Blu Hotel, London Stansted said on Monday 23 November. Companies came from construction, engineering, facilities management, logistics and professional services.

The airport's transformation programme extends the existing terminal with new shops, bars and restaurants, and is meant to let Stansted handle up to 51 million passengers a year without a new runway. Marcella M'Rabety, the airport's head of social sustainability, said it wanted local businesses to share in that investment.

London Stansted launched Meet the Buyers in 2001. The airport says it has helped generate more than £37m of business for East of England firms in the past 15 years, and that Manchester and East Midlands airports have since copied the idea.

Event first held in 2001

stories.headline: Grays drug-driver jailed over death of man, 72, hit by reversing van
stories.summary: Billy Howard-Smith, 26, has been sentenced to 40 months in prison for causing the death of Roy Hibbert in Lodge Lane, Grays.
body: Mr Hibbert was on foot in Lodge Lane on the evening of Monday 21 April 2025 when Howard-Smith reversed a van into him. He died in hospital two months later, on 21 June 2025.

Howard-Smith, of Heathview Road, Grays, was arrested at the scene. Blood tests found a by-product of cocaine in his blood above the legal limit for driving. Essex Police said this showed he had taken the drug at some point before. Officers from the force's Serious Collision Investigation Unit spent more than a year on the case, and he was charged in June.

At Basildon Crown Court on Friday 21 August, he admitted causing death by careless driving while over the specified limit for a drug. He also admitted possessing a Class B drug. He was sentenced on Wednesday 18 November and banned from driving for six years and eight months. Essex Police released details of the case on Monday 23 November.

Detective Richard March, of the Serious Collision Investigation Unit, said his thoughts remained with Mr Hibbert's family. He said the case showed the danger of driving after taking drugs, "even if you think it is no longer in your system".
points: Banned from driving for six years and eight months
Blood tests found a cocaine by-product over the limit
He admitted the charges on 21 August

stories.headline: Colchester Borough Homes wins top MoD award for Armed Forces support
stories.summary: Colchester's council housing company has been given the Gold Award under the Defence Employer Recognition Scheme, the Ministry of Defence's highest honour for employers.
body: Colchester Borough Homes received the award at a ceremony aboard HMS Belfast in London on Thursday 12 November, two years after it won Silver status in 2024. It was one of 11 employers in East Anglia among 162 across the UK to win Gold this year, according to the East Anglia Reserve Forces' and Cadets' Association.

The scheme recognises employers that support serving personnel, reservists, veterans and military families and follow the Armed Forces Covenant. Philip Sullivan, chief executive of Colchester Borough Homes, said several veterans and relatives of serving personnel work for the company, and that supporting the Armed Forces community was a priority in a garrison city.

The awards were presented by Major General John Mark Lancaster, Assistant Chief of Defence Staff for Reserves and Cadets. Colchester Borough Homes manages Colchester City Council's homes, so the commitment covers Armed Forces families as tenants as well as staff.
points: Ceremony held on HMS Belfast on 12 November

stories.headline: Chelmsford rough sleeping rose 50% in four years, council says
stories.summary: Chelmsford City Council's rough sleeping navigators help people off the streets and into housing. They say more people are sleeping rough in the city each year, though the rise is slower than across England.
body: The navigator team was set up in early 2020 with extra government money for areas with more rough sleeping. It told the council's City Life news site on Monday 23 November that fewer than one in ten people it works with need nothing more than somewhere to live. Its leader, Jonathan, who has more than 25 years in housing and homelessness work, described the navigators as the link between the different services. About a quarter of people sleeping rough in Chelmsford did not become homeless in the city.

Most people are referred by park wardens, police, social workers, health staff or the council's homelessness service. Navigators help them get ID, a bank account, a benefits claim and a phone so they can make a formal homelessness application. A panel of providers first agrees who is best placed to house each person. Most then move into supported housing run by the council, housing associations and CHESS, including a former motel turned into 24 furnished flats with round-the-clock support.

Across England, 96% more people slept rough in 2025 than in 2021, against a 50% rise in Chelmsford, the council said. Anyone worried about someone sleeping rough can report them through StreetLink at streetlink.org.uk or its app, which passes the details to the outreach team. The council suggests giving time or money to Sanctus, CHESS or Open Road rather than cash.
points: Navigator team created in early 2020
Fewer than 1 in 10 people need only a home
Report concerns through StreetLink

body: On Saturday 28 and Sunday 29 November buses replace trains from Southend Victoria and from Ingatestone to Newbury Park, the Central line station in east London, and between Southminster and Wickford, Network Rail said. Trains from Norwich, Ipswich and Clacton will run only as far as Shenfield, with passengers changing to replacement buses via Ingatestone. The work includes general maintenance of the Southend Victoria and Southminster line and preparation on the Great Eastern main line ahead of Christmas track work at Forest Gate and Stratford.

stories.headline: Harlow Council on track for fourth budget surplus in a row
stories.summary: The council has kept its share of council tax frozen since 2021, and says its credit rating has been upgraded to AA−.
points: Overall budget up from £173m in 2024/25 to about £350m in 2026/27
Harlow's share of a Band D bill is £288.90 of £2,298.69
Forecast went to the council's Cabinet last week
body: Harlow Council expects to finish 2026/27 with money to spare in its main day-to-day budget for the fourth year running. The forecast is in a financial monitoring report that went to the council's Cabinet last week. The budget in question, the General Fund, pays for most everyday council services, and a surplus means income is expected to more than cover spending.

The council describes the forecast surplus as small but healthy. Over the same period, the council's overall budget, which includes spending on council homes and rebuilding the town centre, has grown from £173 million in 2024/25 to about £350 million in 2026/27.

The council says it ended each of the past three financial years in surplus and met all its key financial tests in 2025/26. It has kept its share of council tax at the same level since 2021, and says an independent credit rating has been upgraded to AA−, putting Harlow ahead of comparable councils.

It puts the results down to making its teams more efficient, cutting costs that add little for residents, reviewing spending regularly, earning more from its commercial property and other assets, and tracking every agreed saving and income target.

Councillor Dan Swords, the council's leader, said: "When residents ask me how we can afford to rebuild the town centre, improve council homes and renew our neighbourhoods, I think the answer starts with how we run the council. Every pound belongs to the people of Harlow. When we cut an unnecessary cost, free up staff time or earn more from a property we own, we can put those resources to work on the things residents have asked us to deliver."

Councillor James Leppard, cabinet member for finance, said: "We take nothing for granted. Delivering a fourth surplus means keeping that discipline right through to the end of the financial year. If costs rise or income falls short, we act early."

The freeze covers only Harlow Council's part of the council tax bill. In 2026/27 its share for a Band D home is £288.90, out of a total of £2,298.69 that also pays for Essex County Council, Essex Police and Essex Fire and Rescue Service, the council's own figures show. The same figures put the council's net borrowing at about £297 million on 31 March 2025.

stories.headline: Greater Anglia and c2c target under-16s as crossing misuse rises 65%
stories.summary: A crossing near Upminster has been shut for almost eight weeks after children were filmed doing handstands and playing chicken with trains.
body: Rail chiefs have launched a safety campaign aimed at 10 to 15 year olds after a sharp rise in children and teenagers putting themselves in danger at level crossings on the lines that serve Essex. GBR Anglia, the joint team running Network Rail Anglia, c2c and Greater Anglia, backed the new phase of the national No Second Chances campaign on Monday 23 November. It warns young people about wearing headphones or looking at phones while crossing, and about filming or playing chicken on crossings.

Network Rail's Anglia route covers the lines out of Liverpool Street and Fenchurch Street through Essex and East Anglia. Its figures show incidents involving young people there rose from 37 in 2017/18 to 61 in 2025/26. More than 2,000 incidents were recorded at Anglia crossings over the past three years, and 153 of them, about 8%, involved under-18s. A further 42 have been logged so far in 2026/27, a provisional figure.

The campaign follows the emergency closure of Brickfields level crossing, just east of Upminster, where a footpath crosses the c2c line through the Cranham Brickfields nature reserve. About 230 trains a day use the line. The crossing was shut on 30 September after a camera survey caught young people doing handstands on the tracks and deliberately playing chicken with oncoming trains. The closure was first set for 21 days but has been extended, and the crossing will stay shut while staff visit local schools.

Shenel Bullock, who leads level crossing safety for GBR Anglia, said when it closed that the railway "cannot ignore the significant risks posed by this behaviour". She urged parents and carers to talk to their children about railway safety.

Across Britain, more than 11,000 safety incidents have been recorded at or near level crossings since 2024, and children and young people account for more than one in ten, Network Rail says. No Second Chances began in April with three 20-second films aimed at 18 to 34 year olds. An earlier level crossing campaign cut near misses by 69% at the crossings it targeted. Daniel Fisk, Network Rail's head of level crossings and public safety, said a familiar crossing "doesn't reduce the risk".

The dangers are well known in Essex. Two teenage girls were killed by a train at the crossing beside Elsenham station in 2005. Network Rail was later fined £1m, built a footbridge and now locks the gates when a train is approaching. In October, GBR Anglia fitted red and green lights and audible warnings at two footpath crossings: Spring Lane, between Hythe and Wivenhoe, and Woodgrange Close, between Southend East and Thorpe Bay.

Network Rail's advice is to stop, look and listen at every crossing, take headphones off, put phones away and cross quickly without stopping. British Transport Police asks anyone who sees unsafe behaviour on the railway to text 61016.
points: 153 of more than 2,000 Anglia crossing incidents in three years involved under-18s
Warning lights fitted in October at crossings near Wivenhoe and Thorpe Bay
Report unsafe behaviour to British Transport Police by texting 61016

stories.headline: Ardleigh to get Environment Agency flood equipment depot
stories.summary: The building on the edge of Colchester will hold the kit crews need when rivers or the sea threaten homes, with call-outs across Essex and Suffolk.
points: Approved by Tendring District Council on Wednesday
Site at the Evolve Business Park in Old Ipswich Road
EA barriers can reach anywhere in England within 12 hours

also.name: Environment Agency blog: temporary flood barriers

body: Tendring District Council approved the plans on Wednesday, as first reported by the Daily Gazette. The Environment Agency applied to build a specialist flood response and incident management depot on greenfield land at the Evolve Business Park in Old Ipswich Road, Ardleigh, just off the A12.

Its application says the depot will only be busy now and then: call-outs come mainly in heavy rain or when the risk of flooding is high. The rest of the time it will store the equipment and keep it ready to go.

Nationally, the Environment Agency says it has 260 mobile pumps, including 17 ultra-high-volume pumps, and 25km of temporary flood barriers that can be sent anywhere in England. It has said its barriers can reach any part of the country within 12 hours. Its own operations teams then put them up where a permanent defence is not possible or has not yet been built.

Graham Verrier, the agency's area director for Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, said earlier this year that £56m of government money would go on 50 flood schemes across the East of England in 2026/27. Anyone can check their flood risk and sign up for free flood warnings at gov.uk/check-flooding.

stories.headline: Wickford derailment repairs to cost Network Rail £3.65m
stories.summary: The bill covers the repairs after a Greater Anglia train came off the rails south of Wickford during August's heatwave. Investigators are still working out why it happened.
body: Network Rail has put the cost of repairing the line south of Wickford at £3.65m, covering heavy machinery hire and track repairs, as first reported by New Civil Engineer and Railnews. Together with £5.4m for the derailment at Lewes in East Sussex the day before, it leaves Network Rail facing a bill of about £9m from two derailments in two days last summer.

The Seax has gone back over the official record of what happened on Friday 14 August. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) says the train, running from Southend Victoria to London Liverpool Street, left the track at about 2.08pm, around 2.1 miles south-east of Wickford station near Salcott Crescent. Its data recorder shows it was doing about 77mph. The driver had seen a kink in the track that rocked the cab and was reporting it when they braked, after an emergency call from a train coming the other way.

For about a mile and a half, the rear coach was dragged across the sleepers and ballast before the train stopped. It stayed upright. Ambulance crews, backed by two air ambulances, checked all 62 people on board and nobody needed hospital. Rayleigh and Wickford MP Mark Francois said the coach acted like a "knife" on the line: about 3,700 sleepers had to be replaced, along with signals and overhead power lines.

The line between Billericay and Hockley stayed shut for 12 days. Passengers took a shuttle train from Shenfield to Billericay, then buses to Wickford, Rayleigh and Hockley. Trains to Southend Victoria ran normally again from Wednesday 26 August, while the Southminster branch stayed on buses until 28 August for planned track renewals.

Investigators have not yet established the cause. The RAIB opened a full investigation on 28 August. It is looking at how the track was maintained, what was done to protect it in hot weather and how it was managed, and will publish a final report when its work ends. Network Rail has said the extreme heat and drought caused exceptional problems for the railway, and dried-out clay led to slower timetables on the Southend Victoria line from 1 September. Jamie Burles, managing director of GBR Anglia, said the operator was sorry for the disruption and thankful no one was hurt.
points: 62 people on board, train doing about 77mph
Rear coach dragged a mile and a half, wrecking 3,700 sleepers
Billericay to Hockley line shut for 12 days
RAIB investigation into the cause still under way

stories.headline: Braintree cat Zeus takes 37-mile solo train trip to Liverpool Street
stories.summary: A Braintree cat got on an evening train by himself. Station staff in London spotted him and sent him home.
body: Zeus, a half-British shorthair, got on the 8.08pm Greater Anglia service from Braintree on Tuesday 10 November, BBC News reported. He made the whole journey to London Liverpool Street alone.

Staff at Liverpool Street spotted him and took him to their office. Greater Anglia staff then travelled back to Braintree with him. His owner, Lily Burroughs, told the BBC her first thought was 'oh my God, he's done it again'.
## A cat with a travel habit

It is not his first trip. Zeus first made headlines in summer 2025, when he boarded a Stansted Express train to the airport, the Bishop's Stortford Independent reported in June. The family then lived in Water Lane, Stansted Mountfitchet. He was a familiar face on the village station platform and in nearby shops and pubs.

In April the family moved to a home about five minutes from Braintree station. Zeus soon made himself at home there too, lounging on the platform steps and in the waiting room and getting fuss from commuters. He is microchipped, wears trackers and has his own Instagram account.
points: Boarded the 8.08pm from Braintree on 10 November
Greater Anglia staff took him home

stories.headline: Thorrington pub wall reunites Colchester man with letter he posted in 1972
stories.summary: A first day cover that Rennie Chivers posted to himself 54 years ago has turned up framed on a wall at the Red Lion in Thorrington.
body: Rennie Chivers, from Colchester, assumed the envelope had been lost long ago. On Friday 20 November, 54 years to the day after its postmark, he found it framed on a wall at the Red Lion in Thorrington, BBC News reported.

His friend of more than 50 years, Nick Dunham, spotted it when the pair stopped for a drink on a walk. A handwritten note beneath it read 'still waiting for Rennie'. Mr Chivers only took notice when he saw his own name on it.
## What a first day cover is

A first day cover is a specially designed envelope carrying newly issued stamps, postmarked on the day they are released. This one carried the 1972 stamps marking the silver wedding anniversary of Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh.
## A pub mystery

The pub's current owners say the envelope was already on display when they took over, so nobody knows how it got there. Landlady Michela Luca said it should stay on the wall as part of the pub's history. She suggested adding a note to say Rennie has now been in. Mr Chivers told the BBC he had 'absolutely no idea' how it ended up there.
points: Found on the anniversary of its postmark
Landlady Michela Luca suggested a note telling its story

body: The biggest moment comes at 10am on Tuesday 24 November, when a public inquiry opens at County Hall, Chelmsford, into the compulsory purchase and side roads orders for the £81m [Army and Navy roundabout scheme](/story/chelmsford-army-and-navy-public-inquiry-compulsory-purchase-24-november/). On the same day London Stansted holds a full-scale [emergency exercise](/story/stansted-airport-emergency-exercise-400-24-november/) with about 400 people from the airport and the county's emergency services. More emergency vehicles than usual will be seen near the airport.

Council business fills the rest of the week. Colchester's Local Plan Committee decides on Monday 23 November whether to recommend sending the [draft plan to the Planning Inspectorate](/story/colchester-local-plan-1800-responses-inspector-submission/) after 1,800 responses. Thurrock Council's Corporate Scrutiny Committee discusses [£27.3m of proposed savings](/story/thurrock-council-27-3m-savings-two-years-72-posts/) on Tuesday 24 November. That evening Basildon Council's Regeneration Scrutiny Committee looks at [£150,000 for town centre safety wardens](/story/basildon-town-centre-community-safety-wardens-150000-s106/), underpass cleaning and lighting. Maldon District Council opens a four-week consultation on the scope of its new Local Plan on Wednesday 25 November. On Thursday 26 November Basildon's cabinet decides on a [rent policy](/story/basildon-council-rent-convergence-extra-1-a-week-april-2027/) adding up to £1 a week for most council tenants from April 2027.

Christmas arrives in earnest on Thursday 26 November. Billericay's Late Night Light Up brings the town's first official lights switch-on since before the pandemic at 5.30pm, and Grays switches on its tree lights from 4.30pm. Light Up Leigh-on-Sea follows from 4pm on Friday 27 November, the day Cinderella opens at Chelmsford Theatre. B&M opens its first [Colchester city centre store](/story/colchester-b-and-m-st-johns-walk-former-wilko-opening/) at St John's Walk on Saturday 28 November, and Mind in West Essex holds its [Merry Minds Festive Fun Run](/story/harlow-merry-minds-festive-fun-run-water-gardens-mind-west-essex/) at Harlow's Water Gardens on Sunday 29 November. Full bids for UK Town of Culture 2028 are due on Monday 30 November, with [Basildon one of 15 towns shortlisted](/story/c-basildon-town-of-culture-phil-redmond-visit/).

body: Customers of every major bank can withdraw and pay in cash, deposit cheques and pay bills there from 9am to 5pm, Monday to Friday. The Mayor of Halstead, Cllr James Bond, will cut the ribbon at a public opening at 10am on Friday 27 November, Essex-TV reports.

Staff from individual banks also see their own customers in private on set days: NatWest on Mondays, Barclays on Tuesdays, Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland on Wednesdays and Thursdays, and Santander on Fridays. Halstead Town Council announced on 12 August 2025 that the temporary hub was open at the church, behind the library. Cash Access UK thanked the church team for hosting it while a permanent home was found.

Cash Access UK chief executive Gareth Oakley said banking and payment habits were changing, which is why it is opening hubs and deposit machines that let small firms bank their cash. LINK, the UK's cash machine network, recommended a hub for Halstead after a request from the community. Six hubs are now open in Essex, with the others in Billericay, Hadleigh, Maldon, Rochford and Saffron Walden.
